claim: Promyrmister kistneri is a fossil beetle found in 99-million-year-old Burmese amber.
source: We describe a fossil beetle in 99-million-year-old Burmese amber that we infer to have been a social impostor of the earliest-known ant colonies. Promyrmister kistneri gen. et sp. nov. belongs to the haeteriine clown beetles (Coleoptera: Histeridae)
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the age of the amber and the taxonomic identity of the fossil.

claim: Promyrmister kistneri belongs to the haeteriine clown beetles (Coleoptera: Histeridae).
source: Promyrmister kistneri gen. et sp. nov. belongs to the haeteriine clown beetles (Coleoptera: Histeridae)
evidence: The taxonomic placement is stated directly in the abstract and supported by morphological analysis.

claim: Haeteriine clown beetles are a major clade of myrmecophiles with specialized adaptations for colony infiltration.
source: Promyrmister kistneri gen. et sp. nov. belongs to the haeteriine clown beetles (Coleoptera: Histeridae), a major clade of 'myrmecophiles'—specialized nest intruders with dramatic anatomical, chemical and behavioral adaptations for colony infiltration.
evidence: The abstract characterizes haeteriine beetles as specialized myrmecophiles, drawing on established knowledge of this group.

claim: Promyrmister evolved close to the emergence of ant eusociality.
source: Promyrmister reveals that myrmecophiles evolved close to the emergence of ant eusociality, in colonies of stem-group ants that predominate Burmese amber, or with cryptic crown-group ants that remain largely unknown at this time.
evidence: The temporal proximity is inferred from the age of the fossil and the known timing of ant eusociality emergence.

claim: The clown beetle-ant relationship has been maintained by beetles host-switching to numerous modern ant genera.
source: The clown beetle-ant relationship has been maintained ever since by the beetles host-switching to numerous modern ant genera, ultimately diversifying into one of the largest radiations of symbiotic animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis and the diversity of modern host associations.

claim: Obligate behavioral symbioses can evolve relatively rapidly and be sustained over deep time.
source: We infer that obligate behavioral symbioses can evolve relatively rapidly, and be sustained over deep time.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fossil evidence and the persistence of the symbiosis.

claim: Approximately 10,000 species are hypothesized to target or profit from ant nests.
source: The diversity of such organisms is impressive, with ~10,000 species hypothesized to target or profit from ant nests alone (Elmes, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Elmes, 1996.

claim: Hostility of ant workers to non-nestmate organisms has selected for defensive or host-deceptive adaptations in myrmecophiles.
source: Hostility of ant workers to virtually all non-nestmate organisms has selected for defensive or host-deceptive adaptations in myrmecophiles which are often phenotypically remarkable, involving changes in anatomy, chemical ecology and behavior (Kistner, 1979; Kistner, 1982; Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990; Parker, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature on myrmecophile adaptations.

claim: Haeteriinae is a subfamily of approximately 335 described species comprising possibly the single largest radiation of myrmecophiles known within the Coleoptera.
source: The clown beetle family Histeridae includes multiple lineages that have independently evolved myrmecophily (Parker, 2016; Kovarik and Caterino, 2005), including Haeteriinae, a subfamily of ~335 described species comprising possibly the single largest radiation of myrmecophiles known within the Coleoptera (Parker, 2016; Kovarik and Caterino, 2005; Helava et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Parker, 2016; Kovarik and Caterino, 2005; Helava et al., 1985.

claim: The clown beetle-ant interaction constitutes the most ancient behavioral symbiosis known in the Metazoa.
source: To our knowledge, the relationship constitutes the most ancient behavioral symbiosis known in the Metazoa.
evidence: This is a claim based on the authors' assessment of the fossil record and known symbioses.

claim: The holotype specimen CNU-008021 is deposited in Key Laboratory of Insect Evolution and Environmental Changes, Capital Normal University, Beijing.
source: Sex unknown. CNU-008021, deposited in Key Laboratory of Insect Evolution and Environmental Changes, Capital Normal University, Beijing.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the specimen repository.

claim: The holotype is well preserved in a small, transparent amber piece measuring 5.5 mm length × 3.5 mm width.
source: The holotype is well preserved in a small, transparent amber piece, 5.5 mm length ×3.5 mm width (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation of the specimen with reference to a figure.

claim: The entire external anatomy of the holotype is observable.
source: The entire external anatomy is observable (Figure 1A‒C), but the left region of the dorsal side is partially covered by white exudate (Figure 1A,G) emanating from the ventral side of the pronotal margin (arrow in Figure 1A,G).
evidence: This is a direct observation with reference to figures.

claim: Promyrmister is distinguished from all other genera and species of Haeteriinae by a combination of specific morphological characters.
source: Haeteriine histerid that is distinguished from all other genera and species of Haeteriinae by possession of the following combination of characters: (1) deep depression behind meso- and metacoxae (Figure 1C,H); (2) metaventral postcoxal line recurved and extending laterally to metanepisternum (Figure 1B,C; (3) three complete striae on each elytron (Figure 1A); (4) lack of dorsal furrows on pronotum demarcating glandular lobe (Figure 1A,B); (5) strongly developed apical spur on protibia (Figure 1D,E); (6) frontoclypeus carinate medially (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C); (7) triangular-shaped cavities to receive scapes of antennae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C); (8) glandular opening in postcoxal cavity behind metacoxae (Figure 1H; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B,D).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of the specimen with reference to multiple figures.

claim: Promyrmister specifically differs from Haeterius in having deep epistomal depressions, carinated epistomal striae convergent in the middle, and paddle-shaped protibia with large apical spur.
source: Promyrmister specifically differs from the closely related Haeterius in having deep epistomal depressions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C; compare to Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), carinated epistomal striae convergent in the middle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C) and paddle-shaped protibia with large apical spur (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis with reference to figures.

claim: The holotype inclusion is derived from an amber mine located near Noije Bum, Tanaing, Kachin, Myanmar.
source: The holotype inclusion is derived from an amber mine located near Noije Bum, Tanaing, Kachin, Myanmar.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the specimen's provenance.

claim: U-Pb dating of zircons from the volcanoclastic matrix yielded an age of 98.79 ± 0.62 million years.
source: The U-Pb dating of zircons from the volcanoclastic matrix yielded an age of 98.79 ± 0.62 million years (Shi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2012.

claim: The name Promyrmister refers to the likely symbiotic habits of the fossil taxon inside early ant colonies.
source: The name refers to the likely symbiotic habits of the fossil taxon inside early ant colonies.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the meaning of the name.

claim: The specific epithet kistneri recognizes the lifetime contribution of Dr. David H. Kistner.
source: The specific epithet recognizes the lifetime contribution of Dr. David H. Kistner, a global authority on social insect symbionts.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the etymology of the species name.

claim: Promyrmister has a body length of 3.2 mm and width of 2.3 mm.
source: Length 3.2 mm, width 2.3 mm.
evidence: This is a direct measurement of the specimen.

claim: Promyrmister has an elongate oval body that is moderately convex.
source: Body elongate oval (Figure 1A,C), moderately convex (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is a direct observation with reference to figures.

claim: Promyrmister is black or dark brown with dorsal surfaces bearing short and somewhat squamiform setae.
source: black or dark brown with dorsal surfaces bearing short and somewhat squamiform setae, visible along pronotal and elytral edges but on dorsal side often obscured by accumulation of water/dirt and appearing as tiny granules
evidence: This is a direct observation of the specimen.

claim: The head of Promyrmister is only partially visible and deeply inserted into the prothorax.
source: Head only partially visible, deeply inserted into prothorax (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation with reference to figures.

claim: The frons of Promyrmister has a distinct frontoclypeal carina.
source: Frons with distinct frontoclypeal carina (FC in Figure 1D)
evidence: This is a direct observation with reference to a figure.

claim: The antennal scape of Promyrmister is large and triangular, covering the eye.
source: Antennal scape large and triangular (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), covering eye, and densely rugose dorsally.
evidence: This is a direct observation with reference to a figure.

claim: The prothorax of Promyrmister is 1.0 mm in length and 1.8 mm in width.
source: Prothorax (length 1.0 mm and width 1.8 mm)
evidence: This is a direct measurement of the specimen.

claim: The prothorax of Promyrmister is widest at the base with weakly rounded sides converging anteriorly.
source: widest at base, sides weakly rounded, converging anteriorly, anterior angles distinctly projecting and rounded; posterior angles weakly obtuse (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation with reference to a figure.

claim: The elytra of Promyrmister are 1.8 mm in length and 2.3 mm in width.
source: Elytra (1.8 mm length ×2.3 mm width)
evidence: This is a direct measurement of the specimen.

claim: Promyrmister has three relatively complete dorsal striae and reduced striae 4-6 on the elytra.
source: with relatively complete dorsal striae 1‒three and reduced striae 4–6 (white arrows in Figure 1A)
evidence: This is a direct observation with reference to a figure.

claim: Promyrmister possesses postcoxal glandular openings behind the metacoxae.
source: Large abdominal gland opening behind hind coxa located between inner and outer abdominal striae (Figure 1H), on right side with exudate flowing out (paired arrows in Figure 1H; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,D, note that laser reflectance indicates this is solidified material and not a gas/air bubble, which would appear dark).
evidence: This is a direct observation with reference to figures.

claim: The fossil beetle is placed in Histeridae based on specific morphological characters.
source: The fossil beetle is placed in Histeridae based on its possession of the following characters (Kovarik and Caterino, 2000): (i) a broad and compact body shape (Figure 1A,C); (ii) striate elytra that expose the two posterior abdominal tergites (Figure 1A); ii) five visible abdominal sternites (Figure 1C); (iv) short legs with broad, flattened tibiae (Figure 1C,E); (v) antenna short and geniculate with compact, 3-segmented club (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B); (vi) antenna retracting into cavity underneath the pronotum (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B); (vii) tarsal formula 5-5-5.
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis with reference to figures and a citation.

claim: Promyrmister can be placed unequivocally in the subfamily Haeteriinae based on specific morphological characters.
source: Of the 11 histerid subfamilies (Bouchard et al., 2011), Promyrmister can be placed unequivocally in the subfamily Haeteriinae based on the following characters: head deflexed, with clypeus arched downwards in a different plane to the vertex (Figure 1D); antenna with enlarged, triangular scape received in repose in frontal groove and hiding the eye (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C); antennal cavities located on hypomeron (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), covered from below by proventral alae; proventral lobe strongly developed anteriorly, covering head from below, and extending laterally to form proventral alae (without lateral notch); proventral keel narrowly elevated between coxae and distinctly emarginate posteriorly to receive the projecting mesoventral process (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis with reference to figures and citations.

claim: The front, mid, and hind legs of Promyrmister are extremely broad, which is a feature of the clade Yarmister + Haeteriinae.
source: Additionally, the front, mid, and hind legs are extremely broad (Figure 1C,E), which is a feature of the clade Yarmister + Haeteriinae (Caterino and Tishechkin, 2015)
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis with reference to a figure and a citation.

claim: Promyrmister possesses a distinctly elevated proventral keel with posterior incision, which is an autapomorphy of the Haeteriinae.
source: in which Yarmister lacks the distinctly elevated proventral keel with posterior incision, which is present in Promyrmister and is an autapomorphy of the Haetaeriinae (Helava et al., 1985).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis with a citation.

claim: Within Haeteriinae, Promyrmister appears to bear a close relationship to the genus Haeterius and some closely allied genera.
source: Within Haeteriinae, the new taxon appears to bear a close relationship to the genus Haeterius Erichson and some closely allied genera that share several morphological characters supporting their monophyly (Yélamos, 1997)
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis with a citation.

claim: Promyrmister shares with Haeterius and allied genera broad and externally rounded tibiae, deep depressions behind meso- and metacoxae, recurved metaventral postcoxal line, and three complete striae on each elytron.
source: principally the broad and externally rounded tibiae, the deep depressions behind meso- and metacoxae to accommodate retracted legs (Figure 1C,H) (Caterino and Tishechkin, 2015), the metaventral postcoxal line being recurved and extending laterally to the metanepisternum (Figure 1B,C), and the presence of three complete striae on each elytron (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis with reference to figures and a citation.

claim: Cladistic and Bayesian analysis places Promyrmister within Haeteriinae as sister to Haeterius.
source: Consistent with our evaluation of Promyrmister's likely phylogenetic placement, both cladistic and Bayesian analysis of a set of morphological characters (Caterino and Tishechkin, 2015) from the fossil specimen and a selection of Recent histerid taxa places the new taxon within Haeteriinae as sister to Haeterius (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis with reference to figures.

claim: Promyrmister represents an extinct Cretaceous lineage that belongs within the crown-group of Haeteriinae.
source: We infer that Promyrmister represents an extinct Cretaceous lineage that belongs within the crown-group of Haeteriinae.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Haeteriine beetles have been shown to engage in intimate behaviors with ants, including stomodeal trophallaxis.
source: In haeteriine taxa for which detailed behavioral observations exist, the beetles have been shown to engage in intimate behaviors with ants, involving stomodeal trophallaxis (mouth-to-mouth feeding) (Wheeler, 1908; Henderson and Jeanne, 1990; Akre, 1968)
evidence: This is supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Haeteriine beetles groom workers with their appendages and are groomed or licked by hosts in return.
source: grooming workers with their appendages (and being groomed or licked by hosts in return) (Akre, 1968)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a behavioral study.

claim: Haeteriine beetles physically grasp onto ants (phoresis) or are carried around nests by workers.
source: physically grasping onto ants (phoresis) (Akre, 1968; von Beeren and Tishechkin, 2017), or being carried around nests by workers (Kistner, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Mimicry of colony cuticular hydrocarbons occurs in haeteriine beetles.
source: Mimicry of colony cuticular hydrocarbons occurs (Lenoir et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a chemical ecology study.

claim: Haeteriine beetles chemically manipulate host ants via 'appeasement' substances exuded from gland openings on the margins of the prothorax or in the postcoxal regions.
source: as well as chemical manipulation of host ants via 'appeasement' substances exuded from gland openings on the margins of the prothorax (Kistner, 1982; Seyfried, 1928) or in the postcoxal regions of the beetle's underside (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to a figure.

claim: Promyrmister appears to be closely allied to the extant genus Haeterius.
source: Promyrmister appears to be closely allied to the extant genus Haeterius (Figure 2A–C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis with reference to figures.

claim: Haeterius and closely related taxa are the only group of Haeteriinae known to occur in the Palaearctic.
source: This genus and a handful of closely related taxa including Eretmotus, Sternocoelis and Satrapes comprise the only group of Haeteriinae known to occur in the Palaearctic, consistent with the Eurasian palaeolocality of Promyrmister in Burmese amber.
evidence: This is based on biogeographic knowledge of the group.

claim: Promyrmister exhibits classical haeteriine attributes that are thought to be true adaptations for myrmecophily.
source: Like all of these genera, Promyrmister exhibits classical haeteriine attributes that are thought to be true adaptations for myrmecophily, including broad expansions of the tibiae with spines on the outer margin (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), short tarsi received on the outer face of each tibia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), a triangular antennal scape (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), pronounced antennal cavities on the prothoracic hypomeron (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) and a broad proventral lobe to fully embrace the retracted head (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis with reference to figures.

claim: The morphological features of Promyrmister are thought to be protective modifications that enable myrmecophile beetles to withstand handling by ant mandibles.
source: Those features are thought to be protective modifications that enable myrmecophile beetles to withstand handling by ant mandibles (Parker, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review on myrmecophiles.

claim: Rove beetles in the Burmese palaeofauna were putative symbionts of termite colonies.
source: We and others have previously described rove beetles (Staphylinidae) in the Burmese palaeofauna that were putative symbionts of termite colonies (Yamamoto et al., 2016; Cai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The rove beetle specimens from Burmese amber exhibit a defensive ecomorphology and are thought to have been persecuted intruders not behaviorally integrated into their host's societies.
source: These specimens exhibit a defensive ecomorphology and are thought to have been persecuted intruders that were not behaviorally integrated into their host's societies (Yamamoto et al., 2016; Cai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Haeteriinae embody a form of true behavioral symbiosis where the relationship with host ants can involve social interactions.
source: In contrast, Haeteriinae embody a form of true behavioral symbiosis, where the relationship with host ants can involve social interactions (Figure 2D,E; Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on behavioral observations with reference to figures.

claim: In the Promyrmister holotype, a large globule of possible exudate originates from the left margin of the prothorax, consistent with the position of prothoracic glands.
source: The prothoracic glandular openings of Haeteriinae that secrete putative appeasement compounds are challenging to demonstrate even in extant taxa, but in the Promyrmister holotype, a large globule of possible exudate originates from the left margin of the prothorax, consistent with the position of such glands (Figure 1A,G).
evidence: This is a direct observation with reference to figures.

claim: Promyrmister possesses clear postcoxal secretory glands with a globule of possible exudate emanating from the postcoxal gland opening on the right side of the body.
source: Additionally, Promyrmister possesses clear postcoxal secretory glands (Figure 1H; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B,D), with a globule of possible exudate emanating from the postcoxal gland opening on the right side of the body (Figure 1H; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,D).
evidence: This is a direct observation with reference to figures.

claim: Promyrmister's anatomy implies a chemical strategy to become accepted or at least tolerated inside colonies, akin to modern haeteriine species.
source: Beyond Promyrmister's phylogenetic position within the Haeteriinae clade, the fossil's anatomy implies a chemical strategy to become accepted or at least tolerated inside colonies (hypothetical reconstruction in Figure 2F), akin to modern haeteriine species that have so far been examined (Akre, 1968; Lenoir et al., 2012; Seyfried, 1928).
evidence: This is an inference based on morphological analysis and comparison with modern species, supported by citations.

claim: All ants thus far described from Burmese amber belong to stem-group Formicidae.
source: All ants thus far described from Burmese amber belong to stem-group Formicidae, including members of the extinct subfamily Sphecomyrminae and three other genera, Gerontoformica, Myanmyrma and Camelomecia that similarly lack crown-group features but are placed incertae sedis within Formicidae (Barden, 2016; Barden, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to taxonomic studies.

claim: Fossils of definitive crown-group ant subfamilies are absent, or vanishingly rare, among the thousands of ant inclusions recovered from Burmese amber.
source: In contrast, fossils of definitive crown-group ant subfamilies are absent, or vanishingly rare, among the thousands of ant inclusions now recovered from this amber deposit (Barden, 2016; McKellar et al., 2013) (P. Barden, personal communication).
evidence: This is supported by citations and personal communication.

claim: Crown-group ants are unknown from contemporaneous Charentese amber.
source: Crown-group ants are also unknown from contemporaneous Charentese amber (Barden, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The overwhelming prevalence of stem-group ants in Burmese amber implies that they were potential hosts of Promyrmister.
source: We posit that the overwhelming prevalence of stem-group ants in Burmese amber implies that they were potential hosts of Promyrmister (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the fossil record.

claim: Haeteriines may have originated with stem-group ant colonies and later switched to crown-group ants.
source: Such a scenario entails that haeteriines may not have originated with the modern ant groups that host them today; instead myrmecophily evolved first in stem-group ant colonies, with the beetles later switching to crown-group ants.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the fossil record and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: An alternative scenario is that an as-yet undiscovered diversity of crown-group ants were present in the Burmese palaeofauna and selected for the early evolution of myrmecophily.
source: We cannot, however, rule out an alternative scenario, that an as-yet undiscovered diversity of crown-group ants were, in fact, present in the Burmese palaeofauna, and it was these that selected for the early evolution of myrmecophily.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative hypothesis.

claim: Molecular dating indicates that crown-group ants had originated by the time of Promyrmister.
source: Molecular dating indicates that crown-group ants had originated by this time (Brady et al., 2006; Moreau and Bell, 2013; Borowiec et al., 2017a) (see dotted lines in Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by citations to molecular dating studies.

claim: The original hosts of haeteriines are presumably long-extinct.
source: Whether haeteriines evolved in stem- or crown-group ant colonies, their original hosts are presumably long-extinct.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fossil record and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The present-day host associations of haeteriines imply that these myrmecophiles have host-switched between many modern ant lineages.
source: The present-day host associations of haeteriines imply that these myrmecophiles have host-switched between many modern ant lineages (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on the diversity of modern host associations.

claim: Haeteriine beetles have been recorded in colonies of ant species across the subfamilies Dolichoderinae, Dorylinae, Formicinae, Myrmicinae and Ponerinae.
source: The beetles have been recorded in colonies of ant species scattered across the subfamilies Dolichoderinae, Dorylinae, Formicinae, Myrmicinae and Ponerinae (Helava et al., 1985; Tishechkin, 2007) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by citations to taxonomic and ecological studies.

claim: The capacity for host switching may explain the great longevity of the clown beetle-ant symbiosis.
source: We suggest that it is this capacity for host switching that may explain the great longevity of the clown beetle-ant symbiosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the evolutionary history of the symbiosis.

claim: Through host switching, haeteriines have circumvented potential coextinction with host ant lineages that disappeared from the Cretaceous to the present.
source: Through host switching, the clade as a whole has circumvented potential coextinction with host ant lineages that disappeared from the Cretaceous to the present (Barden and Grimaldi, 2016; Barden, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the evolutionary history of the symbiosis, supported by citations.

claim: The vast majority of the contemporary species richness of Haeteriinae is found in taxa that have adapted to colonies of Neotropical army ants (Ecitonini).
source: Moreover, in some cases, the beetles have radiated dramatically with certain ant groups: the vast majority of the contemporary species richness of Haeteriinae is found in taxa that have adapted to colonies of Neotropical army ants (Ecitonini), including at least 30 genera associated with Eciton army ants alone (Parker, 2016; Helava et al., 1985; von Beeren and Tishechkin, 2017; Tishechkin, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to taxonomic and ecological studies.

claim: Neotropical army ants are thought to have begun diversifying approximately in the Oligocene.
source: Neotropical army ants are thought to have begun diversifying approximately in the Oligocene (Brady et al., 2014; Borowiec et al., 2017b)
evidence: This is supported by citations to molecular dating studies.

claim: The bulk of haeteriine cladogenesis occurred within the Oligocene window, long after the beetles originated in the Cretaceous.
source: implying that the bulk of haeteriine cladogenesis occurred within this window too, long after the beetles originated in the Cretaceous.
evidence: This is an inference based on molecular dating of host ants.

claim: An ancient association between histerids and ants is further suggested by inquiline-like morphology in two other Cretaceous clown beetle fossils.
source: An ancient association between histerids and ants is further suggested by inquiline-like morphology in two other Cretaceous clown beetle fossils (Caterino et al., 2015; Caterino and Maddison, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to other fossil studies.

claim: The taxonomic affinities of two other Cretaceous clown beetle fossils are ambiguous and they are not definitive members of wholly symbiotic lineages.
source: although unlike Promyrmister, the taxonomic affinities of these specimens are ambiguous and they are not definitive members of wholly symbiotic lineages.
evidence: This is a statement about the taxonomic uncertainty of other fossils.

claim: Haeteriinae was a relatively diverse clade by at least the beginning of the Upper Cretaceous.
source: We infer that Haeteriinae was a relatively diverse clade by at least the beginning of the Upper Cretaceous
evidence: This is an inference based on the fossil record.

claim: Haeteriinae likely originated and began undergoing basal cladogenesis very soon after the inferred Early Cretaceous emergence of ant eusociality.
source: and likely originated and began undergoing basal cladogenesis very soon after the inferred Early Cretaceous emergence of ant eusociality (Barden and Grimaldi, 2016; Grimaldi and Agosti, 2000; Barden, 2016; Brady et al., 2006; Moreau and Bell, 2013; Borowiec et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is an inference based on the fossil record and molecular dating, supported by citations.

claim: Rapid evolution of specialized symbiotic phenotypes appears to be a common feature to clades of social insect symbionts.
source: However, based on such analyses for other myrmecophile taxa, rapid evolution of specialized symbiotic phenotypes appears to be a common feature to clades of social insect symbionts (Moore and Robertson, 2014; Parker and Grimaldi, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on other myrmecophile taxa.

claim: Rapid evolution of specialized symbiotic phenotypes presumably results from intense selection pressures inside colonies.
source: and presumably results from intense selection pressures inside colonies (Kistner, 1979; Parker, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations.

claim: Promyrmister adds further support to the view that the earliest-known ants were socially complex.
source: Promyrmister adds further support to the view that the earliest-known ants were socially complex (Barden and Grimaldi, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of a myrmecophile, supported by a citation.

claim: The earliest-known ant colonies were resource rich enough for exploitation by impostor myrmecophiles.
source: Evidently, their colonies were also resource rich enough for exploitation by impostor myrmecophiles
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of Promyrmister.

claim: Myrmecophiles have been an unremitting part of ant biology.
source: which we conclude have been an unremitting part of ant biology.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the fossil evidence.

claim: Complex behavioral relationships between animals can be extraordinarily ancient and persist over deep evolutionary time.
source: Despite their phenotypic intricacy and obligate dependency on other species, complex behavioral relationships between animals can be extraordinarily ancient, and persist over deep evolutionary time.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study.

claim: The holotype specimen is embedded in a cuboid amber piece.
source: The holotype of the new genus and species is embedded in a cuboid amber piece.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the specimen preparation.

claim: The holotype was examined under a Leica M205C dissecting microscope.
source: The holotype was examined under a Leica M205C dissecting microscope
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methods used.

claim: The holotype was photographed using a Visionary Digital BK Lab Plus system.
source: and photographed using a Visionary Digital BK Lab Plus system (Austin, Texas).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methods used.

claim: Fluorescence images of the fossil were made on a Zeiss LSM 880 confocal microscope with a 488 nm laser.
source: Fluorescence images of the fossil were made on a Zeiss LSM 880 (with Airyscan) confocal microscope (Germany) with a 488 nm laser.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methods used.

claim: Promyrmister was scored for 259 external morphological characters used by Caterino and Tishechkin (2015).
source: We scored Promyrmister for 259 external morphological characters used by Caterino and Tishechkin (2015) in a study investigating relationships among the tribe Exosternini, which is closely related to Haeteriinae.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the phylogenetic methods used.

claim: The final taxon list for phylogenetic analysis included 46 taxa.
